lesson_title: Vinegar vs Battery Acid: the Two-Axis Secret
hook_text: Your kitchen vinegar is MORE concentrated than the acid in a pool-test kit. So why is the pool acid scarier?
clip_script: Here's a chemistry plot twist: the vinegar in your kitchen is more concentrated than the hydrochloric acid in a pool-testing kit. More acid molecules per litre. And yet the pool acid is the fiercer one. How? Because chemistry runs acids on two separate axes, and mixing them up is the classic mistake. Axis one: concentration — how much is dissolved. That's just how much syrup you poured in the glass. Axis two: strength — willingness. Drop a strong acid in water and EVERY molecule splits, handing over its proton instantly. A weak acid like vinegar's ethanoic acid? Only a tiny fraction splits; the rest floats intact, holding on. So vinegar is concentrated but weak. Pool drops are dilute but strong. Battery acid is both — that's why it gets the skull on the label. And the bench can't be fooled: at the same concentration, the strong acid shows a lower pH, conducts electricity better, and fizzes harder on magnesium — three symptoms, one cause: more ions in the water. Chemists even write the willingness as a number, K a. Big K a, eager splitter. Tiny K a, reluctant. Two axes. Never let them blur — and half this topic is already yours.
visual_style: Split-screen showdown of a vinegar bottle and a pool-test dropper with axis bars sliding under each — amount versus willingness; molecule animations of total splitting versus reluctant partial splitting; three bench tests flashing pH paper, a glowing bulb and fizzing magnesium.
pacing: Hook on the vinegar reveal, fast axis explainer, rhythmic three-symptom montage, clean two-axes outro.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and never confuse strong with concentrated again.
